# Release Hardening for AI-Assisted Products

How to harden your release process when software is written or co-authored by AI coding tools.

## TL;DR

AI-generated code has a mean vulnerability rate of **55.8%** across 7 major LLMs [2], and existing SAST tools miss **97.8%** of formally-proven vulnerabilities [2]. Meanwhile, **43%** of AI code that passes QA/staging still fails in production [27]. Traditional release gates provide a false sense of security.

Organizations need defense-in-depth: layered controls at pre-merge, post-merge, and production stages. No single tool or process addresses the full risk surface.

## Key Findings

| Metric | Value | Implication |
|--------|-------|-------------|
| Mean vulnerability rate (7 LLMs) | 55.8% [2] | More than half of AI code has provable vulnerabilities |
| SAST miss rate (Z3-proven vulns) | 97.8% [2] | Traditional quality gates are insufficient |
| AI vs human issues per PR | 1.7x [7] | AI code needs more review, not less |
| Production failure (post-QA) | 43% [27] | Pre-production testing misses nearly half of issues |
| Package hallucination (open-source/commercial) | 21.7% / 5.2% [6] | 1 in 5 open-source model suggestions doesn't exist |
| AI review suggestion adoption | 16.6% [11] | AI code review is rejected 5x more than human review |
| Security prompt improvement | 4 percentage points [2] | Telling AI "be secure" barely works |

## Quick Decision Framework

1. **Check your SAST reliance.** If CodeQL/Semgrep is your primary gate, you have a 97.8% blind spot for AI code [2].
2. **Measure AI code volume.** Below 10% you can absorb risk via review. Above 30% you need dedicated hardening.
3. **Layer defenses.** SAST (known patterns) + LLM self-review (78.7% detection [2]) + PBT/mutation testing + canary deployment + production observability.
4. **Fix the human factor.** 25-30 min review intervals, pair programming for high-risk, smaller PRs [14].
5. **Track regulations.** EU AI Act GPAI rules are live. ISO 42001 is the emerging vendor baseline [30].
